title: Starting a Child Care Program in Nebraska: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction

Starting a Child Care Program in Nebraska represents a meaningful opportunity to serve children from infancy through school age while building a compliant, sustainable care business. The need is undeniable, with state data revealing a shortage of over 17,000 child care slots and entire counties lacking any licensed providers. Oversight and funding are administered by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), which manages the state’s licensing and subsidy programs.

With a documented gap of over 17,000 child care spaces, significant state and federal funding allocations, and reimbursement rates ranging from $6.00 to $45.00 per day per child, Nebraska offers a market with significant unmet demand for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. The state’s commitment is further evidenced by over $72 million in Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) funds and additional Head Start funding, creating a supportive financial ecosystem for quality-focused entrepreneurs.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Child Care Program in Nebraska, from understanding the Nebraska child care regulations and licensing to staffing, securing funding, and preparing for inspections. Whether you envision a small family home or a large-scale center, this framework will provide the clarity needed to succeed.

Section 1: Understand Nebraska’s Child Care Program Regulations

Before you can serve a single child, you must have a firm grasp of the regulatory landscape. Nebraska regulates Child Care Programs through the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), which is responsible for licensing and regulation of child care centers, group homes, and family homes to ensure the health, safety, and well-being of children in care. Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations must also comply with federal frameworks like the Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) requirements, Head Start Program Performance Standards, and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

The state’s regulatory framework emphasizes quality, safety, and adherence to strict staff-to-child ratios. Key compliance areas include staff qualifications and background checks, safe environments, nutrition standards, emergency preparedness, and developmentally appropriate programming. Licenses are not a one-time event; they typically require renewal every one to two years, contingent upon successful inspections and adherence to all DHHS rules.

Navigating these detailed requirements can be complex. Understanding the nuances of Title 391 of the Nebraska Administrative Code is essential for a smooth licensing process and long-term operational success.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Your next step is to decide on the specific model that aligns with your vision and resources. Nebraska supports multiple Child Care Program variants, each with different licensing, staffing, and physical plant requirements. Your choice will directly impact your startup costs, revenue potential, and daily operations.

Nebraska’s primary license types include:

  • Family Child Care Home I & II: These programs are operated in a provider’s private residence. A Family Child Care Home I can care for up to 6 children, while a Family Child Care Home II can care for 7-12 children with an additional staff member. This model offers lower startup costs and a home-like environment.
  • Group Child Care Home I & II: Often located in a separate residence or commercial space, these programs serve a slightly larger group. A Group Child Care Home I is licensed for 7-12 children, while a Group Child Care Home II can serve up to 15 children.
  • Child Care Center: This is the largest model, licensed for 16 or more children in a dedicated commercial facility. Centers are required to have more structured administration, including a qualified Program Director, and must meet more stringent facility and staffing regulations.

Program size typically ranges from 3 children in a small family home to over 100 in a large center. Demand is strongest in the ten rural counties that currently have no licensed providers and for specialized niches like infant care, bilingual programs, and care for children with special needs across the state. While urban centers like Omaha and Lincoln have more providers, they also have long waitlists, particularly for infants. Conversely, underserved rural counties may offer significant entry opportunities with less direct competition.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Once you’ve chosen your program type, you must establish the legal and administrative foundation for your business. This is a critical step in obtaining your Nebraska child care license. Providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC), S-Corporation, or a Non-Profit organization.

To become an official business entity and apply for a license, you must:

  • Register your business name and structure with the Nebraska Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and tax purposes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability insurance and, if you have employees, workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Submit a complete licensing application to the Nebraska DHHS. This application is extensive and requires detailed information about your program, facility, staff, and policies.

Be prepared for a thorough process. Licensing timelines in Nebraska generally range from 4 to 9 months, depending on the completeness of your application, the time required for background checks, and the scheduling of your initial facility inspection. A well-prepared application is the fastest way to approval.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A solid business plan is your roadmap to financial sustainability. It will help you secure funding, manage expenses, and set realistic revenue goals. Understanding the Nebraska child care startup costs and operational financials is key.

Startup costs in Nebraska typically range from $5,000 for a small Family Child Care Home to over $150,000 for a newly constructed Child Care Center. These costs cover licensing fees, facility renovations, purchasing equipment and supplies, insurance, and initial marketing. Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which often represents 50-60% of total costs.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Nebraska include:

  • Child Care Subsidy: Daily reimbursement rates vary by the child’s age, the type of facility, and your location. Rates can be as low as $6.00-$12.00 per day for infants in family homes and up to $45.00 per day for older children in centers.
  • Step Up to Quality Bonus: Providers who achieve a rating in Nebraska’s quality rating and improvement system, “Step Up to Quality,” can earn a 5% increased reimbursement rate, rewarding investment in higher standards.
  • Private Pay: Many providers charge private pay rates that are higher than the state subsidy, especially in higher-income areas or for specialized services like infant care.

With diligent management, providers operating at a target occupancy of 70-80% can generally achieve 5-15% profit margins. The report indicates a typical break-even timeline of 12 to 18 months, making financial planning and enrollment projections critical from day one.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical location must be safe, accessible, and compliant with all DHHS regulations. Whether you are using your own home or a commercial building, the environment is a core component of your license.

Key facility requirements you must meet include:

  • Minimum Square Footage: Nebraska mandates a specific amount of usable indoor and outdoor space per child to prevent overcrowding.
  • Safety and Sanitation: The facility must be free of hazards. This includes having covered electrical outlets, secure storage for cleaning supplies, lead-free paint, and functioning smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.
  • Adequate Restrooms and Sinks: You must have a sufficient number of toilets and handwashing sinks accessible to both children and staff.
  • Fenced Outdoor Play Area: A secure, fenced outdoor space is required for physical activity, equipped with safe, age-appropriate play structures.
  • Kitchen and Food Service: If you provide meals, your kitchen must meet health department standards for food storage, preparation, and sanitation.
  • Accessibility: The facility must be compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), ensuring access for children and parents with disabilities.

When selecting a location, consider local zoning laws, proximity to residential neighborhoods and elementary schools, accessibility for parents’ commutes, and the availability of a qualified workforce in the area.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your program. Nebraska’s regulations set clear standards for staff qualifications, background checks, and ongoing training to ensure children are cared for by competent and trustworthy individuals. The Nebraska child care requirements for staffing are non-negotiable.

Required roles for a child care program typically include:

  • Program Director (for Centers): Must meet specific educational and experience requirements in early childhood education or a related field.
  • Lead Teachers: Responsible for a specific group of children and for planning and implementing the curriculum.
  • Assistant Teachers/Aides: Support Lead Teachers in supervising children and carrying out daily activities.
  • Support Staff: May include cooks, administrative assistants, and janitorial staff, all of whom must also pass background checks if they have contact with children.

All staff members with direct access to children must undergo a comprehensive background check, including state and federal criminal history checks and child abuse registry checks. Required training includes First Aid and CPR certification, Safe Sleep practices for infant care staff, Mandated Reporter training for child abuse and neglect, and a minimum number of annual continuing education hours in topics like child development, health, and safety.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Written policies and procedures are the operational backbone of your child care program. They ensure consistency, promote safety, and are a mandatory part of your licensing application. Nebraska requires providers to develop and maintain a comprehensive policy manual that is available to staff and parents.

DHHS requires written policies covering key areas such as:

  • Health and Safety: Emergency plans for fire, tornadoes, and medical emergencies; illness policies; medication administration.
  • Enrollment and Admission: Non-discrimination statements, enrollment forms, and disenrollment procedures.
  • Behavior Guidance: Positive discipline techniques and prohibited actions.
  • Supervision: Staff-to-child ratios for all age groups and activities, including naptime and outdoor play.
  • Nutrition: Meal and snack menus, allergy management, and safe food handling.
  • Parent Communication: Policies for daily communication, parent conferences, and resolving grievances.
  • Transportation: Procedures for transporting children, if applicable.

In addition to facility-wide policies, individual care or service plans must be developed for each child, outlining their specific needs, allergies, developmental goals, and emergency contacts. These plans must be regularly reviewed and updated in partnership with parents.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

With a significant child care shortage in Nebraska, your marketing focus should be less on broad advertising and more on building trust and connecting with key referral sources. Your compliance and quality of care are your best marketing tools.

Referrals for new child care programs in Nebraska typically come from:

  • Nebraska Child Care Referral Network: A state-supported service that connects parents with licensed providers.
  • Local DHHS Offices: Social workers and case managers often refer families receiving child care subsidies.
  • Large Local Employers: Many companies are seeking reliable child care options for their employees and may partner with or refer to local centers.
  • Pediatricians and Family Health Clinics: Medical professionals are a trusted source of recommendations for parents.
  • Local School Districts: Especially for before- and after-school care programs.
  • Online Presence: A professional website and active social media pages (especially local parent groups on Facebook) can build credibility and attract private-pay families.
  • Word-of-Mouth: Happy parents are your most powerful advocates.

Successful providers focus on building a reputation for reliability, safety, and excellent communication. Hosting an open house before you open can generate initial interest and help you start building a waitlist.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Oversight is ongoing and includes unannounced inspections from licensing specialists from the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). These inspections are designed to ensure you are consistently meeting all regulatory standards.

Inspectors focus on health and safety, and common deficiencies often include:

  • Incorrect staff-to-child ratios during certain parts of the day.
  • Incomplete or outdated staff files, such as missing background checks or training certificates.
  • Environmental safety hazards like cleaning supplies within reach of children or unsafe playground equipment.
  • Improper documentation, including attendance records, fire drills, or incident reports.
  • Failure to follow safe sleep practices for infants.

To stay prepared, implement a system of continuous quality improvement. Conduct regular self-audits, maintain meticulous records, and ensure all staff are consistently trained on your policies. Keeping your facility and documentation “audit-ready” at all times is the best way to ensure smooth inspections and maintain your license in good standing.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a Child Care Program in Nebraska?

A: The timeline can vary, but it typically takes 4 to 9 months from submitting a complete application to receiving your license. The break-even point for a new business is often between 12 and 18 months of operation.

Q: What licenses are required to open a child care business in Nebraska?

A: You must obtain a license from the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). The specific license type depends on your capacity: Family Child Care Home (3-12 children), Group Child Care Home (7-15 children), or Child Care Center (16+ children).

Q: What reimbursement is available for child care in Nebraska?

A: Reimbursement is available through Nebraska’s Child Care Subsidy program, funded by the federal CCDBG. Daily rates vary from $6.00 to $45.00 per child based on age, program type, and location. Additionally, providers can earn a 5% reimbursement bonus by achieving a quality rating through the “Step Up to Quality” system.

Conclusion

Starting a Child Care Program in Nebraska is a challenging but incredibly rewarding venture that addresses a critical community need. The path to success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of DHHS regulations, and a steadfast commitment to operational discipline. Providers who invest in creating a safe, high-quality environment, hiring and training excellent staff, and building strong relationships with families and referral sources are positioned for long-term success and a positive impact on Nebraska’s next generation.
